name: Ireland (since 1922)
summary: Most of Ireland became independent from the UK as the Irish Free State in 1922 and a republic in 1949; Northern Ireland remained in the UK.

knownFor.label: Celtic Tiger
knownFor.note: Fast economic growth from the mid-1990s.

knownFor.label: Easter Rising
knownFor.note: The 1916 rebellion that led to independence.

location.value: Most of the island of Ireland; about 70,000 km².

terrain.value: Central lowlands ringed by hills; Atlantic coast.

climate.value: Mild and wet all year, shaped by the Atlantic and the Gulf Stream; winters are rarely below freezing and rain falls on about 150–225 days a year.

resources.value: Rich grassland for cattle and dairy, peat bogs once burned for fuel, fish, and offshore gas (Corrib field); few metals apart from zinc and lead mines.

disasters.value: Atlantic storms and coastal and river flooding; the Great Famine (1845–52) happened before independence but still shapes memory.

urbanisation.value: About two-thirds live in towns; Greater Dublin has around 1.5 million people, followed by Cork, Limerick and Galway.

disease.value: Life expectancy is over 82 years; the public and private health systems are both used, and waiting lists are a long-running political issue.

wealth.value: One of the highest incomes per person in the EU, partly because multinational companies book large profits in Ireland; ordinary household income is lower than the headline figures suggest.

moneyAndTax.value: Used the Irish pound (punt) until the euro arrived in 2002; a low 12.5% company tax rate attracted US technology and drug firms.

inequality.value: Income gaps after taxes and benefits are close to the EU average; high rents and house prices are the biggest pressure on young people.

governmentType.value: A parliamentary republic: the Taoiseach (prime minister) leads the government; the elected President is head of state with limited powers.

keyRulers.value: Michael Collins. Éamon de Valera. Mary Robinson.

succession.value: Governments are formed after elections to the Dáil, using proportional representation with a single transferable vote; coalitions are common.

institutions.value: The Oireachtas (Dáil and Seanad), an independent Supreme Court that can strike down laws, and a written constitution (1937) changed only by referendum.

stability.value: Civil War (1922–23) over the treaty with Britain; peaceful and democratic since, though the Northern Ireland Troubles (1968–98) affected the Republic too.

eliteConflict.value: Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael, both born from the Civil War split, led most governments; Sinn Féin has grown strongly since 2020.

armyAndTech.value: Small Defence Forces of under 10,000; known for long service in UN peacekeeping missions, especially in Lebanon.

majorWars.value: War of Independence against Britain (1919–21), then the Civil War (1922–23); neutral in the Second World War (“the Emergency”).

territoryChange.value: The island was partitioned in 1921: six northern counties stayed in the UK as Northern Ireland; the 1998 Good Friday Agreement dropped the Republic’s territorial claim.

alliancesRivals.value: Militarily neutral and not in NATO; joined the European Communities in 1973; close but sometimes tense ties with Britain, especially over Brexit and the Irish border.

inventions.value: Irish-born scientists include Robert Boyle and William Thomson (Lord Kelvin), from before independence; modern Ireland is a hub for software and medical devices.

scienceEducation.value: Free secondary education since 1967; around half of young adults hold a degree, among the highest shares in Europe.

openness.value: One of the most open economies in the world: exports and imports are worth more than its GDP, and foreign firms employ hundreds of thousands.

communicationTransport.value: Motorways built in the 2000s, Dublin’s Luas trams and DART railway, and busy airports in Dublin, Shannon and Cork.

religion.value: Mostly Catholic (about 69% in 2022), but church attendance has fallen sharply; voters legalised same-sex marriage (2015) and abortion (2018).

languageWriting.value: Irish (Gaeilge) is the first official language and taught in all schools, but English is spoken by almost everyone; Irish is spoken daily in Gaeltacht areas.

artsArchitecture.value: World-famous writers (Joyce, Yeats, Beckett, Heaney), traditional music and dance, and Georgian Dublin architecture.

socialStructure.value: A large middle class; Irish Travellers are a recognised ethnic minority; about one in five residents was born abroad.

sharedIdentity.value: Irish identity rests on independence, Gaelic games (hurling, Gaelic football), music and the Irish language.

dailyLife.value: Most people live in houses; tea, brown bread, Irish stew and the pub play a big part in social life.

neighbours.value: Its only land border is with Northern Ireland (UK); Britain lies across the Irish Sea.

ideasReligions.value: A diaspora of perhaps 70 million people of Irish descent, mainly in the US, Britain and Australia, spread Irish culture worldwide.

colonisation.value: Ruled by England, then Britain, for centuries; part of the United Kingdom from 1801 to 1922.

riseSignals.value: Easter Rising (1916), the War of Independence and the Anglo-Irish Treaty led to the Irish Free State in 1922 and a republic in 1949.

peakPeriod.value: The “Celtic Tiger” boom (about 1995–2007), when fast growth ended centuries of emigration.

declineSignals.value: The 2008 property and banking crash led to an EU–IMF bailout (2010) and a wave of emigration.

overallCertainty.value: Well documented by official statistics and many histories; figures on company profits distort GDP, so other income measures are used.
